⚖️ 'A Prohibition Taking Effect on a Prohibition' — Rav Asi's resolution of a self-contradicting baraita

overview.title: 📖 Overview: How Much of What Counts?
overview.subtitle: Meilah 16a–16b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Building on yesterday's mishna that all carcasses combine for their measure, the Gemara asks whether that combination extends to the prohibition of EATING carcasses, not merely to ritual impurity. Rav, Levi, and Rav Asi stake out different positions, tested against baraitot about a dead cow and a live camel in every possible combination — resolved through the principle of whether a prohibition can 'take effect' on an item already forbidden by another prohibition. The daf then turns to creeping animals: Rav says one is flogged for eating an olive-bulk, but a baraita praised by Rabbi Yoḥanan suggests a smaller lentil-bulk suffices — reconciled first by distinguishing live from dead creatures, and then, after further challenges, by limiting the lentil-bulk rule to the eight specific creeping animals the Torah singles out.

slides.title: 🐄 Do Kosher and Non-Kosher Carcasses Combine for Eating?
slides.subtitle: Three amoraic positions on the mishna's scope

lines.speaker: Rav
lines.text: The mishna's rule that all carcasses combine applies only to ritual IMPURITY. For the prohibition of EATING, kosher carcasses combine only with other kosher carcasses, and non-kosher only with non-kosher.

lines.speaker: Levi
lines.text: Even for EATING, kosher and non-kosher carcasses combine together to reach the liability measure.

lines.speaker: Rav Asi
lines.text: Kosher carcasses combine only among themselves; non-kosher only among themselves — though it's unclear whether he means this for impurity too, or agrees with Rav there and disagrees only about eating.

callout.label: Why it matters:
callout.text: The dispute turns on whether 'carcass' is one unified category for every purpose, or whether the EATING prohibition specifically singles out kosher animals (already forbidden once dead) differently from non-kosher animals (forbidden even alive).

slides.title: 🐫 Testing Every Combination: Cow and Camel
slides.subtitle: Baraitot probing exactly which pairings combine
rows: Half olive-bulk dead cow + half olive-bulk LIVE camel
Baseline case in the first baraita
Half olive-bulk LIVE cow + half olive-bulk LIVE camel
Both share the prohibition on eating a limb from a living animal, which applies even to non-kosher animals
Half olive-bulk LIVE cow + half olive-bulk DEAD camel
From the second baraita's first clause
Half olive-bulk cow + half olive-bulk camel, EITHER alive or dead
From the second baraita's second clause — creates an apparent internal contradiction

callout.label: The puzzle:
callout.text: The second baraita's own two clauses seem to contradict each other — resolved next through the concept of 'a prohibition taking effect on a prohibition.'

slides.title: ⚖️ Rav Asi's Resolution: Issur Chal Al Issur
slides.subtitle: Does the carcass prohibition 'add on' to an already-forbidden non-kosher animal?

steps.content: 1️⃣ Non-kosher meat is already forbidden to eat, whether alive or dead — so does the ADDITIONAL 'carcass' prohibition (which applies once an animal dies) take effect on top of that pre-existing prohibition?

2️⃣ The tanna of the contradictory baraita holds YES — a prohibition CAN take effect on an already-prohibited item — so the carcass prohibition applies equally to cow and camel, letting their dead flesh combine

3️⃣ Rav Asi himself holds NO — a prohibition does NOT take effect where another already exists — so a non-kosher camel's flesh is governed only by its ORIGINAL non-kosher-animal prohibition, never by the separate carcass prohibition
4️⃣ Result: since cow and camel are then governed by two DIFFERENT prohibitions, their flesh never combines — Rav Asi's view survives, unthreatened by this baraita

slides.title: 🦎 Olive-Bulk or Lentil-Bulk for Eating Creeping Animals?
slides.subtitle: Rav's rule tested, defended, and eventually narrowed

nodes.content: 📏 Rav: one is flogged for eating creeping animals only at an OLIVE-BULK — since 'eating' language always implies that measure
⚡ Challenge: a baraita (praised by R' Yoḥanan!) derives from Lev. 20:25 that eating shares its measure with IMPURITY — a LENTIL-bulk, smaller than an olive-bulk
🔄 First resolution: Rav's olive-bulk applies to LIVE creeping animals; the lentil-bulk baraita speaks of DEAD ones (which also transmit impurity)
⚡ Abaye's counter: but our very mishna (combining sheratzim) implies even DEAD ones need an olive-bulk for lashes — Rav Yosef dismisses this as Abaye's own inference, not Rav's actual intent

✅ Final resolution (Rava): R' Yoḥanan's lentil-bulk rule applies ONLY to the EIGHT specific creeping animals the Torah singles out (מוּבְדָּלִין) — all OTHER creeping animals still need a full olive-bulk

slides.title: 🔟 Rav Adda bar Ahava Pushes the Logic Further
slides.subtitle: If the eight special creeping animals get their own measure, why not kosher vs. non-kosher too?

lines.speaker: Rav Adda bar Ahava
lines.text: If Rabbi Yoḥanan's lentil-bulk rule is limited to the eight singled-out creeping animals, shouldn't the same logic apply to ANIMALS? Leviticus 20:25 juxtaposes kosher animals with creeping animals too — so kosher carcasses (a distinct, Torah-recognized category) should have one measure, and non-kosher carcasses (not distinguished by the Torah as edible) a DIFFERENT, larger measure — perhaps an egg-bulk.

lines.speaker: Setup for Rava
lines.text: The challenge presses Rava to explain whether his 'eight special creatures' principle is a narrow textual detail, or reflects a broader pattern that should also reshape the rules for kosher and non-kosher animal carcasses.

callout.label: Open thread:
callout.text: This challenge sets up the continuing analysis of exactly how far the Torah's distinctions among forbidden foods reach into their measured liability.

summary.principle: Whether different forbidden foods combine to reach a liability measure depends on whether they share one underlying prohibition or fall under separate ones (issur chal al issur), and the Torah's own textual distinctions — like the eight singled-out creeping animals — can carve out narrower or different measures within a single broad category.

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: measures for forbidden foods track precise textual categories — Torah wording, not intuition, sets exactly what combines with what

quiz.q: According to Rav, does the mishna's rule that 'all carcasses combine' apply to the prohibition of eating them?
o: Yes, kosher and non-kosher carcasses always combine for eating
No — that rule applies only to ritual impurity; for eating, kosher carcasses combine only with kosher, and non-kosher only with non-kosher
The mishna doesn't discuss eating at all
Rav says carcasses never combine for any purpose
quiz.e: Rav limits the mishna's combination rule to ritual impurity, holding that the eating prohibition treats kosher and non-kosher carcasses as separate categories.

quiz.q: How does Rav Asi resolve the apparent contradiction between two clauses of a baraita about combining cow and camel flesh?
o: He rejects the baraita as unreliable

He explains that the contradictory clause follows a view that a prohibition CAN take effect on an already-prohibited item, while he himself holds it cannot — so the cases are governed by different, non-combining prohibitions
He says cow and camel can never be compared
He says the baraita is discussing a different topic entirely
quiz.e: Rav Asi attributes the seemingly contradictory ruling to a tanna who holds that a new prohibition can take effect atop an existing one, which is not his own position — so the baraita doesn't actually contradict his view.

quiz.q: What is Rav's rule for the minimum amount of creeping animals (sheratzim) one must eat to be liable for lashes?
o: A lentil-bulk
An olive-bulk, since the term 'eating' in the Torah always implies that measure
An egg-bulk
There is no minimum measure
quiz.e: Rav Yehuda cites Rav's rule that eating creeping animals requires an olive-bulk for lashes, based on the general principle that scriptural 'eating' implies that specific measure.

quiz.q: How does Rava ultimately reconcile Rabbi Yoḥanan's apparent endorsement of a lentil-bulk measure for eating creeping animals with Rav's olive-bulk rule?
o: He says Rabbi Yoḥanan was mistaken
He limits the lentil-bulk rule to only the eight specific creeping animals the Torah singles out; all other creeping animals still require an olive-bulk
He says both measures apply equally to all creeping animals
He says the lentil-bulk rule applies only to impurity, never to eating, with no exceptions
quiz.e: Rava's resolution restricts Rabbi Yoḥanan's lentil-bulk ruling to the eight creeping animals explicitly enumerated in the Torah, preserving Rav's olive-bulk rule for all others.

quiz.q: What does Rav Adda bar Ahava suggest as a parallel implication of Rava's 'eight special creeping animals' principle?
o: That all creeping animals should have identical measures
That kosher and non-kosher animal carcasses might likewise need different measures for imparting impurity or triggering the eating prohibition, since they too are distinguished by the Torah
That impurity laws should be abolished for animals
That Rava's principle applies only to birds, not animals
quiz.e: Rav Adda bar Ahava extends Rava's logic — since the Torah juxtaposes kosher/non-kosher animals with creeping animals in the same verse — to ask whether kosher and non-kosher carcasses should likewise have distinct measures.
